s01b01.text: Welcome to the Warehouse Training Packet. Over the next twenty minutes we will walk through how freight is received, how parts are packaged, stored and shipped, how orders and returns are handled, how inventory is counted, and how we keep the warehouse clean, well maintained and safe.

s01b02.text: Why does this matter? The packet puts it simply. Warehouse personnel help manage one of the company's largest assets, the spare parts inventory. The accuracy of everything we do contributes to the credibility of that inventory.

s01b03.text: Our customers rely on the availability of our spare parts to keep their machines operating. Accurate inventory and timely, accurate work build their confidence in our ability to serve them. And when everyone does their own area accurately and on time, the whole company becomes more efficient.

s01b04.text: The packet also summarises the most common errors. They typically relate to the timely processing of documentation. Managing parts inventory means processing every activity on time, storing, stocking, shipping, counting, and the paperwork that goes with each.

s01b05.text: To avoid those errors, understand the impact each task has on the inventory, follow the required instructions, and ask for assistance in any area you are not familiar with. This packet cannot cover every task, so never hesitate to ask your supervisor.

s01b06.text: Here is the road ahead. Six parts, from the receiving dock to safety. Let's begin where the inventory begins, at the dock.

s02b01.text: Receiving of freight is the beginning point of spare parts inventory management. Get this step right and everything downstream, stocking, filling and counting, gets easier.

s02b02.text: Before anything else, a safety rule with no exception. Every delivery truck must have its wheels chocked. Make sure the delivery drivers know this. Every truck, every time.

s02b03.text: Incoming freight is unloaded and inspected for damages and shortages before the manifest is signed. Shipments are counted and compared to the shipping manifest that comes with them. This must be done before signing the carrier's receipt.

s02b04.text: If you find damage, note it on the manifest. Then follow the carrier's guidelines for filing a freight claim. Timeliness and proper documentation are critical to processing a claim, and taking photos can be very helpful in noting and settling it.

s02b05.text: Freight then goes to the designated area for sorting between stock orders and emergency orders. The two have different clocks. Stock orders are checked and put in their proper locations within twenty-four hours after receiving.

s02b06.text: Emergency orders are checked in within two hours after receiving, because customers and shop orders are waiting on them. Freight charges are then determined and added to the shop and customer orders.

s02b07.text: For emergency orders going to the shop or to customer destinations, the proper packing slips are printed and attached to the shipment. Air shipments come through UPS and FedEx.

s02b08.text: Paperwork then goes to the Inventory Analyst to input into the computer system, which updates the inventory on hand. And every day, all incoming and outgoing paperwork is filed in the appropriate folders for future reference.

s02b09.text: Chock, inspect and count, sign, sort, check in on time, document, file. That is receiving.

s03b01.text: Parts arrive in different types of packaging, and each type must be identified and handled properly. The packet describes three.

s03b02.text: Multiple packaged parts are parts with more than one in the package. For example, a package may hold a quantity of ten, but the parts are sold as individual units.

s03b03.text: Parts packed in sets consist of two or more identical pieces that together make a quantity of one set. Two brake shoes, for example, make one set.

s03b04.text: Parts packed in kits consist of multiple different parts and quantities that make one kit. A cylinder seal kit, for example, contains seals, seal bearings and oil bearings, and together they reseal or rebuild one hydraulic cylinder.

s03b05.text: Now, storing. Warehouse space is almost always limited, so efficient use of it is critical. Stacked cartons should plainly display the part number. That makes order filling quicker and helps avoid pulling errors.

s03b06.text: Avoid stocking multiple parts in the same location. When it cannot be avoided, make sure the parts are dissimilar. Every bin location is clearly marked with the correct part number, and any bin label that is damaged, partially missing or worn gets replaced.

s03b07.text: When parts are stored outside, the carton must be weatherproof enough to protect what is inside. Moisture from condensation can cause rust and damage to parts stored inside closed crates or cartons.

s03b08.text: Proper stocking looks like this. Every part placed in stock has a visible part number on the part or carton. All part numbers face front in racks and shelving. Overstock locations are clearly tagged, so overstock is used before pulling from the permanent location.

s03b09.text: Process all discrepancies within the established guidelines and time frames. Remove unnecessary tags, wire, tape and strapping. And make it clear whether a part is sold individually or in package quantity.

s03b10.text: Prevent improper stocking. Never overstock a location. If it is not large enough, have the location changed. Never overload wire baskets or shelves. Make sure the part number and description match the part being stocked. Do not remove protective packaging that guards against rust, dirt and weather. And store parts with machined surfaces so those surfaces are protected.

s04b01.text: Each warehouse has a layout based on the type and size of the parts it holds. As a new employee you will become familiar with that layout and help stock parts in a way that supports the location system.

s04b02.text: Two things make a location system easy to use. All aisles are properly marked and easy to identify. And sections within a row are clearly marked, so you can find the proper location quickly. Any question about proper stocking goes to the Parts or Warehouse Supervisor.

s04b03.text: The mezzanine is intended for lighter, slower moving inventory, and for storing supplies, packing material and cartons.

s04b04.text: It is kept to the same high standard of cleanliness as the main warehouse. Shelves stay free of dust and organised to the same practices. And every weight limitation is clearly marked and followed.

s04b05.text: Packing and shipping is where customers see our professionalism. If a customer does not receive all the parts they ordered, or the order is incorrect, the company's image suffers.

s04b06.text: Each part is plainly marked or tagged with the part number and quantity. Clean boxes and packaging are used for every customer shipment. And know the cut off times for each shipper, so orders are processed in time to make them.

s04b07.text: Do not over pack a carton in a way that creates a safety hazard or makes it hard for the customer to handle. Everyone has different lifting limits. As a general rule, a single carton should not exceed fifty pounds, though that can vary with the size, shape and dimensions of the part.

s05b01.text: Part three, ordering and returns. Processing stock orders is a critical step in getting the proper parts to the customer at the proper time. The goal is all received stock on the shelf, with on-hands current, within eight hours of receipt.

s05b02.text: Each item arrives with a vendor's pick tag. Let's read it together.

s05b03.text: Location is the bin where the part is to be placed. Sorting the parts by bin location before shelving can speed up the whole stock order.
s05b03.issues: slight robotic text-to-speech cadence, unnatural pause after location

s05b04.text: Part Number is the vendor's part number. Verify it against the other parts already on the shelf and against the bin tag at that location.

s05b05.text: Pick quantity is the number of pieces for this part on this stock order. Verify it against the parts you actually received. If the quantity does not match, note it on the packing list and give it to the Parts Manager.

s05b06.text: Description should match the physical part. If the tag says bearing and you received bolts, that is a claim discrepancy. Note it on the packing list for the Parts Manager. Item is the item number on the packing list, for a quick cross check.

s05b07.text: Once the parts are compared to the packing list and placed on the shelf, hand the packing list, with any noted discrepancies, to the Parts Manager.

s05b08.text: Order filling works from the pick document. Parts are listed in location sequence, so follow the list and you walk the warehouse once. Filled orders are placed at their destination, Will Call, Shop or Field, or Outbound shipment, and marked.

s05b09.text: If a part or its container appears used, crushed or damaged in any way, inspect it before shipment to verify the customer will receive what is expected. That may mean repackaging.

s05b10.text: When you pull one or more parts from a part stocked in package quantity, empty all the remaining parts into the bin and dispose of the packaging material.

s06b01.text: Accepting returns from customers is an important part of the business. When processing a credit, first review the condition of the package. Broken packages, broken seals or soiled packages go to the attention of the Parts Manager.

s06b02.text: Verify the quantity, description and condition of the parts being returned. Be cautious of cores. It is easy to mistake a core for a new part. And know the return policy for the parts in front of you. The criteria vary by vendor and type of part.

s06b03.text: Vendor returns are handled much like filling a customer order, except there may be tags to remove. A vendor return has two portions, shipping back all of a particular part number, and a partial shipment. Pull the return as directed by the Parts Manager.

s06b04.text: Part four, inventory counts. Properly conducting the scheduled cycle counts and the end of year physical count validates how well the company manages its spare parts inventory. Refer to the Inventory Count policy, and take questions to the local Parts or Warehouse Supervisor.

s06b05.text: If you find a part while counting, note it, and give the part number, description and quantity to the Parts Manager for research.

s06b06.text: The attached cycle count guidelines add detail. Before the weekly count, all stock is put away and receipted, credit returns are shelved, and orders to be pulled are done. Receive the count report from the Parts Manager, count without viewing the computer on-hands, and write the physical count on the count sheet.

s06b07.text: While counting, look around the count area for anything that needs improvement in warehousing practice, and note it on the count sheet to address afterwards. Then enter the counts into the system exactly as counted.

s06b08.text: Items that do not match in on-hand or dollar value go on a recount report. When recounting, take extra care to find the cause. Check the locations in and around the part, and look for credits, stock orders or orders not yet processed.

s07b01.text: Part five, maintenance, starting with housekeeping. Good housekeeping supports a safe work environment, a professional appearance to those who work in or view the area, efficiency and accuracy in our tasks, and protection of the company's assets.

s07b02.text: Daily requirements. Floors and dock areas are swept and trash picked up and disposed of. Cabinets and shelves are dusted. All trash cans are emptied at end of shift, and no trash is left in the warehouse after hours.

s07b03.text: Floor areas are kept clear of oil and liquid spots and spills. And the hose press area is cleaned, with excess hose put back in its proper location after each use.

s07b04.text: To prevent untidy conditions, keep empty boxes and bags out of storage locations, and keep trash like coffee cups and cans picked up. Remove banding from the pallet as soon as it is cut and dispose of it, so nobody is cut or trips on it.

s07b05.text: Broken pallets are replaced and thrown away, so a pallet cannot collapse and injure someone. Broken and splintered pieces are disposed of properly. Overflow parts are never stocked on aisle floors; overflow moves to an assigned, marked area. And fire hydrants, door passageways and electrical junction boxes are kept clear and accessible.

s07b06.text: Vehicle and equipment maintenance keeps productivity high, operating cost low, and the workplace safe. Operate every piece of equipment with respect for others and for the machine itself. Speed or abuse of equipment is not tolerated.

s07b07.text: Daily inspections are conducted, and needed repairs are scheduled by severity. If a repair is safety related, or would sacrifice the health of the machine, the unit is tagged out and not used until the repair is complete. Unsafe equipment is reported to the supervisor immediately.

s07b08.text: Vehicles are kept clean inside and out. Before operating one, complete a visual inspection and report any damage to your supervisor. If the tank is below half full, fill it, so the next person gets a quick start. Everyone is task trained on the equipment they use.

s08b01.text: One more factor in your success is your own attitude, toward your job, your fellow workers, your customers and the company's goals. A good attitude is contagious. It builds relationships with customers and co-workers that help everyone succeed. Your attitude is yours to own and manage.

s08b02.text: Your appearance sends a message too. Keep it neat and clean, and avoid wearing anything that could be hazardous around machinery. Keep growing your knowledge of the profession, notice changes in the business, and find better ways to do the work. And tell your supervisor your career goals, so you can plan the skills you need.

s08b03.text: Part six, safety. Safety is everyone's responsibility, and every employee is expected to work safely. Attending the weekly safety meeting, completing annual refresher training, and wearing the proper personal protective equipment are expectations, not options.

s08b04.text: Know how to safely operate every tool and piece of equipment. Serious injury can come from improper lifting, so follow the guidelines for bending, lifting and twisting when moving parts, and ask for assistance when a lift exceeds what should be expected.

s08b05.text: Forklifts and other material handling equipment require proper training in their operating practices, and only authorised employees operate equipment or vehicles. Improper use of hand tools is one of the largest causes of warehouse injuries, so use caution with box cutters and knives.

s08b06.text: Parts classified as hazardous material require special stocking, shipping and handling. Be familiar with the Hazardous Material Safety Data Sheets and the proper stocking practices. Building hydraulic hoses also requires specific training on hose presses, hose saws and stocking hydraulic parts. Training will be provided in all of these areas.

s08b07.text: Some general rules. No horseplay. Observe all safety and traffic signs. Keep unauthorised personnel out of designated areas. Good housekeeping is part of the job. Tools, equipment and materials are kept in good working order, and anything damaged or broken is removed from service.

s08b08.text: The right personal safety equipment is used for each task, and it is the supervisor's responsibility to provide it. Equipment or vehicles being repaired are locked out and tagged out. And every employee must know the location, operation and proper use of the emergency equipment.

s09b01.text: Let's recap. Receive, store and ship. Order, fill and return. Count. Maintain. Stay safe.

s09b02.text: Quick check. A truck backs up to the dock. What must happen before unloading begins? Its wheels are chocked. No exception.

s09b03.text: An emergency order has just arrived. How long do you have to check it in? Two hours. Stock orders have twenty-four.

s09b04.text: You find a worn, partly missing bin label. What do you do? Replace it. Every bin is clearly marked with the correct part number.

s09b05.text: A forklift has a safety related fault. What happens? It is tagged out, not used until the repair is complete, and reported to the supervisor immediately.

s09b06.text: You pull two parts from a package of ten. What happens to the other eight? They are emptied into the bin, and the packaging is disposed of.

s09b07.text: Thank you for taking the time to learn how this warehouse runs. Accuracy and timeliness in your work keep the inventory credible and our customers' machines running. When a question comes up, visit your supervisor. Welcome to the team.

s09b06a.text: You are packing a customer order and the carton is getting heavy. As a general rule, what is the most a single carton should weigh? Fifty pounds. It can vary with the size, shape and dimensions of the part, and the carton must stay safe and easy to handle.

s09b06b.text: A pick tag says bearing, but the box you received holds bolts. What do you do? That is a claim discrepancy. Note it on the packing list, and give the packing list to the Parts Manager.

s09b06c.text: You are about to do a weekly cycle count. Should you look at the computer on-hands first? No. Count without viewing the on-hands, write the physical count on the count sheet, and enter it into the system exactly as counted.

s09b06d.text: A carton is heavier than you expected. How do you move it safely? Follow the lifting guidelines for bending, lifting and twisting, and ask for assistance when the lift exceeds what should be expected. Serious injury can come from improper lifting.
